articles.author: Kathlene Joyce C. Ramones
articles.title: From small towns to big markets: La Union trade fair turns silver
articles.body:
Before La Union’s local products reached the shelves and shopping bags of Metro Manila consumers, they first had to find a market beyond the province.

In 2001, La Union brought its woven goods, native delicacies, and handicrafts to the capital in an early effort to introduce products made by small-town entrepreneurs to a much bigger market.

Twenty-five years later, that initiative has grown into La Union’s Fairest, an annual trade and tourism fair that continues to provide local enterprises with opportunities to expand their market reach and connect with consumers beyond their communities.

The fair opened its 25th edition on November 4 at the Grand Atrium of Shangri-La Plaza Mall in Mandaluyong City, featuring 51 micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) representing all 20 component local government units of La Union.

Running until November 8, the five-day showcase brings together producers of local delicacies, woven goods, handicrafts, and artworks, providing them with a venue to introduce their products to consumers outside their hometowns.

Governor Mario Eduardo Ortega led the opening ceremony and ribbon-cutting, joined by provincial officials and trade representatives.

He recognized those who started the initiative and encouraged participating entrepreneurs to continue improving their products.

“We continue what others started before us,” Ortega said.

A vision that started with local products

The fair began during the early implementation of the One Town, One Product (OTOP) program, when provincial leaders brought La Union’s homegrown products to Manila to test their potential in a wider market.

Board Member Maria Rosario Eufrosina “Chary” Nisce recalled how the initiative provided local producers with their first opportunities to introduce their goods to consumers outside the province.

Since then, the fair has grown into an annual showcase of enterprises from across La Union, reflecting the continuing efforts to promote local products and support small businesses.

Its silver anniversary also recognized five MSMEs that have participated in every edition since 2001.

Their continued involvement reflects the opportunities they have pursued and the growth they have experienced alongside the fair.

From local shelves to wider markets

For the Halog West Producers Cooperative in Tubao, joining the fair in 2017 marked an important step in bringing its signature chichacorn to Metro Manila.

Cooperative manager Ireneo Zaldo Panes recalled how participating in the event helped increase sales and introduce their product to customers beyond La Union.

For community-based enterprises, however, accessing buyers in major commercial centers can be challenging.

Trade fairs provide a venue where small producers can display their goods, meet potential customers, and establish business connections without the costs of maintaining a permanent presence in the city.

The opportunities extend beyond food and traditional crafts.

This year’s fair also features works by local artists, giving La Union’s creative industry a place alongside its homegrown products.

Jerome Barbadillo of Imaris Art Studio, a participant for the third consecutive year, brought selected works by members of the Artists Guild of La Union (AGLAUN) and other local painters.

The studio also holds live painting workshops, allowing mallgoers to witness the creative process and engage with the province’s visual arts.

Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Ilocos Regional Director Merlie Membrere reaffirmed the agency’s commitment to helping regional enterprises access bigger markets and establish connections with potential buyers and business partners.

The measure of 25 years

The value of the fair, she said, can be seen not only during the event but also in the business opportunities created, markets reached, and enterprises that continue to grow afterward.

“La Union’s Fairest is not just a story of the past. It is a continuing commitment to our entrepreneurs, our communities, and the generations who will carry the La Union spirit forward,” she said.

Twenty-five years since its first run, La Union’s Fairest continues to provide local producers with an avenue to bring their products beyond their immediate markets.

For the entrepreneurs who return each year, the fair offers another opportunity to introduce their products, connect with potential buyers, and bring new business prospects back to their communities.

As it marks its silver anniversary, the fair carries forward the vision that started in 2001: giving homegrown enterprises the opportunity to be recognized, reach wider markets, and contribute to the economic development of their communities.

articles.author: Rey Anthony Chiu
articles.title: Bohol town trades rice for plastic waste as LGUs turn trash into building materials
articles.body:
TAGBILARAN CITY, Bohol (PIA) — In Tubigon town, residents can trade a kilo of shredded plastic wrappers for a kilo of rice, an exchange the municipal government said has reduced clogging in the town’s drainage system.

The shredded plastics go to a private facility, where they are heat-pressed into construction panel boards, plastic lumber, ceiling panels, and non-load-bearing wall cladding.

Tubigon’s program was among the local initiatives showcased at the Bohol Solid Waste Management Summit 2026, organized by the provincial government’s Ecological Solid Waste Management Program.

The annual summit brings together the provincial government, municipalities, national agencies, businesses, and civil society groups to share practices in waste segregation, composting, recycling, resource recovery, safe disposal, and reducing single-use plastics.

Bohol’s waste management policy is anchored on Republic Act No. 9003, or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, which requires local governments to shift from collecting mixed garbage to segregation, recycling, and composting.

Gov. Erico Aristotle Aumentado reconstituted and expanded the Provincial Ecological Solid Waste Management Board through Executive Order No. 38, signed Dec. 26, 2025, to coordinate these efforts across the province.

The local efforts support national campaigns to keep plastic waste out of waterways.

The Marcos administration is enforcing the Extended Producer Responsibility Act of 2022, which requires large companies to recover a rising share of their plastic packaging waste—reaching 60% this year.

Malacañang said the enforcement aims in part to keep garbage from clogging drainage and pumping facilities.

From trash to building materials

In Jagna, workers at the town’s eco park and recycling facility turn shredded plastic bottles and crushed glass into bricks and cobblestones.

Jagna has run an integrated solid waste management program since 2006.

The town also sells its plastic waste to a cement plant in Cebu, which burns it as fuel in place of part of the coal or petroleum coke its kilns traditionally use.

Bags from old tarpaulins

Community groups are turning discarded tarpaulins into handbags.

Groups doing this include the Bunacan Bag Weavers Association, the Tagbilaran City Livelihood and Community Development Unit, and communities assisted by the Presidential Commission for the Urban Poor.

Tagbilaran City’s upcycled eco-bags are now supplied to department stores in Manila, the city’s livelihood unit said.

The summit also featured the Sangguniang Kabataan of Bien Unido and the Women’s Welfare Organization, along with recycling technologies and industrial equipment that local governments can use in their waste operations.
